Japanese whiting (Sillago japonica) is a commercially important coastal species distributed throughout the temperate waters of East Asia. Field surveys conducted in the Seto Inland Sea have provided comprehensive life-history data for this species, with individuals attaining a maximum fork length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm], a size that represents the upper bound of the species' asymptotic growth trajectory. This ultimate length is attained after several years of steady somatic expansion, with the most rapid linear growth occurring during the juvenile phase following metamorphosis from the pelagic larval stage. In this population, puberty is reached at a fork length of 15 cm [Lp = 15 cm], which typically corresponds to the second year of life in waters averaging 21.3 °C [T = 21.3 °C]. The 15 cm [Lp = 15 cm] fork length threshold marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence, after which individuals become reproductively active and begin to participate in the annual spawning aggregations that characterise this species' breeding ecology.

A detailed examination of the reproductive biology of Japanese whiting reveals that females are highly fecund, with a single spawning event yielding up to 68,900 eggs [N_R_i = single spawning event yielding up to 68,900 eggs] when water temperatures remain stable at 21.3 °C [T = 21.3 °C]. This substantial clutch size reflects an adaptive strategy common among marine teleosts that produce pelagic eggs, wherein high fecundity compensates for elevated rates of egg and larval mortality in the planktonic environment. Over the course of a typical spawning season, each mature female produces one clutch annually [F_R_i = one clutch annually], a frequency that appears to be constrained by the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and the seasonal availability of zooplanktonic prey required for larval survival. The combination of a large fecundity per spawning event and a single annual reproductive bout [F_R_i = event and a single annual reproductive bout] places Japanese whiting among the moderate- to high-output iteroparous spawners within the Sillaginidae family, comparable to congeneric species such as Sillago sihama.

The early life stages of Japanese whiting are characterised by rapid embryogenesis and a notably brief egg stage. At the ambient temperature of 21.3 °C [T = 21.3 °C], the fertilised ovum undergoes cleavage, blastulation, and gastrulation within a remarkably short window, with the yolk-sac larva emerging from the chorion after only 4.5 days [ab = 4.5 days]. This age at birth (4.5 days) [ab = 4.5 days] from fertilisation is among the shortest recorded for sillaginid fishes, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritises rapid development to reduce the window of vulnerability for the demersal egg stage at a temperature of 21.3 °C [T = 21.3 °C]. Upon hatching, the prolarva measures approximately 1.5 mm in total length and possesses a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00015 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00015 grams], a calculation derived from the egg diameter of 0.66 mm observed in the closely related Sillago sihama. The newly emerged larva depends entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the initial phase of the yolk-sac larval stage.

As development proceeds through the larval and juvenile phases, Japanese whiting exhibits a steady increase in body mass that culminates in an ultimate wet weight of 201.9 grams [Wwi = 201.9 grams] for fully grown adults. This asymptotic mass (201.9 grams) [Wwi = 201.9 grams] is derived from the length-weight relationship characteristic of the species, in which body mass scales as a power function of fork length, and it represents the maximum somatic investment an individual can achieve under the prevailing food availability and metabolic constraints of its coastal habitat. The transition from the actively growing juvenile phase to the sexually mature adult stage is marked by a deceleration in mass gain as resources are increasingly channelled into gonadal development and reproductive effort. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the ultimate wet weight of 201.9 grams [Wwi = 201.9 grams] is typical for a fish attaining a fork length near 30 cm [Li = 30 cm], with variation across populations primarily driven by differences in water temperature and prey density.

The natural lifespan of Japanese whiting has been documented through mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age estimation, revealing a maximum longevity of 2,190 days [am = 2,190 days] at the local water temperature regime of 21.3 °C [T = 21.3 °C]. This lifespan (2,190 days) [am = 2,190 days] corresponds to approximately six years, with wild individuals rarely exceeding this upper boundary due to natural mortality from predation and senescence at a temperature of 21.3 °C [T = 21.3 °C]. The species' semelparous potential is limited, as most individuals spawn repeatedly over several seasons before reaching the terminal stages of physiological decline. In comparison to the closely related Sillago sihama, which inhabits more tropical waters, Japanese whiting exhibits a slightly extended maximum duration of life, a pattern consistent with the general latitudinal trend toward longer lifespans in cooler thermal regimes. The combination of a six-year maximum longevity (2,190 days) [am = 2,190 days], a moderate age at puberty, and high annual fecundity positions this species within a life-history continuum well adapted to the variable but productive coastal ecosystems of the northwestern Pacific at a temperature of 21.3 °C [T = 21.3 °C].
